what_it_does: Data deduplication is the process of scanning a large dataset to find and eliminate duplicate chunks, which saves storage space — but doing this requires reading enormous amounts of data and moving it back and forth between memory and the processor, which is slow and energy-hungry. A class of hardware called Processing-in-Memory (PIM) — chips that can do simple computations directly inside the memory module, drastically reducing how far data must travel — could help, but comes with its own constraints: units cannot easily share data with each other, and sending results back to the main processor is costly. PIMDup maps the deduplication pipeline onto a real commercial PIM product called UPMEM (which embeds small processors inside standard memory modules), re-engineering the chunking algorithm to avoid operations that PIM handles poorly (like multiplication), and minimizing the data sent back to the host processor. The paper claims 100% correctness of results while achieving meaningful speedup. Specific performance numbers and comparisons should be verified in the full paper.
